But just thinking theoretically about it, what makes the Amaravati
deck better? It seems to have more moving parts. Amaravati is a

record to put it on par with Amaravati. Until enough people try,
though, it's all just speculative.

Not all decks tie their bloat and other defensive options directly
into their ousting mechanism. If a deck separates the two, it means
that a temporary failure of offense doesn't lead more or less directly
to being ousted, because it can fall back and regroup. If a deck
combines the two, it gets the benefit of streamlining, but if it's
offense fails, its defense necessarily does the same.

> To me, a glass cannon says "I hope I don't run into combat.  I bet I
> won't, so I'll win."  A deck built to say "Mwuahahaa, foolz!  Your
> combat is useless against me!  Lulz!" does not seem to fit the model.

We're talking about two different things, then. The definition of
"glass cannon" I've always seen has nothing to do with combat, except
maybe tangentially.

A glass cannon is a deck that's all offense and no/little defense, and
which relies on oust-bloat in order to outrace its predator. The
classic examples are Setite stealth/bleed and Baali stealth/bleed,
since both have Death Star-like offensive capabilities but few ways to
prevent being ousted if they're not getting oust-bloat. In other
words, it's a glass (fragile in the face of other folks ousting it)
cannon (capable of blasting other folks off the table).

As an example of someone else using the term this way:

http://preview.tinyurl.com/55etsl (newsgroup post by Emmit Svenson)

Hopefully that makes my terminology a little more understandable.

John Eno

The Scorpion and the Frog
One day, a scorpion looked around at the mountain where he lived and
decided that he wanted a change. So he set out on a journey through
the forests and hills. He climbed over rocks and under vines and kept
going until he reached a river.

The river was wide and swift, and the scorpion stopped to reconsider
the situation. He couldn't see any way across. So he ran upriver and
then checked downriver, all the while thinking that he might have to
turn back.

Suddenly, he saw a frog sitting in the rushes by the bank of the
stream on the other side of the river. He decided to ask the frog for
help getting across the stream.

"Hellooo Mr. Frog!" called the scorpion across the water, "Would you
be so kind as to give me a ride on your back across the river?"

"Well now, Mr. Scorpion! How do I know that if I try to help you, you
wont try to kill me?" asked the frog hesitantly.

"Because," the scorpion replied, "If I try to kill you, then I would
die too, for you see I cannot swim!"

Now this seemed to make sense to the frog. But he asked. "What about
when I get close to the bank? You could still try to kill me and get
back to the shore!"

"This is true," agreed the scorpion, "But then I wouldn't be able to
get to the other side of the river!"

"Alright then...how do I know you wont just wait till we get to the
other side and THEN kill me?" said the frog.

"Ahh...," crooned the scorpion, "Because you see, once you've taken me
to the other side of this river, I will be so grateful for your help,
that it would hardly be fair to reward you with death, now would it?!"

So the frog agreed to take the scorpion across the river. He swam over
to the bank and settled himself near the mud to pick up his passenger.
The scorpion crawled onto the frog's back, his sharp claws prickling
into the frog's soft hide, and the frog slid into the river. The muddy
water swirled around them, but the frog stayed near the surface so the
scorpion would not drown. He kicked strongly through the first half of
the stream, his flippers paddling wildly against the current.

Halfway across the river, the frog suddenly felt a sharp sting in his
back and, out of the corner of his eye, saw the scorpion remove his
stinger from the frog's back. A deadening numbness began to creep into
his limbs.

"You fool!" croaked the frog, "Now we shall both die! Why on earth did
you do that?"

The scorpion shrugged, and did a little jig on the drownings frog's
back.

"I could not help myself. It is my nature."

Then they both sank into the muddy waters of the swiftly flowing
river.

I don't think that a better player has great chances of winning if his
deck isn't better than the others unless other players are really bad
(so he can convince them to do what he wants). His chances are
somewhat higher, since he is better player, but not very much. Let's
say that on the 5-player table he has 40% chance to win, while the
other 4 players have 15% chance.
When a good player plays a true Tier1 deck against worse decks and
worse players, his chances to win is more than 50%. Actually, he can
be stopped only by the united efforts of several players.

>
> Tier 1 should read - An untrained Ape could win with it.

There is no contradiction - yes, an untrained ape also can win with
some Tier1 decks, though its chances will be lower than the chances of
the good player.

> If the deck has the necessity to require an excellent player in
> performing above standard it isn't Tier 1 imho.
There are some Tier1 decks that aren't suitable for newbs - especially
Wall decks where you have to bluff, to choose what you will block, and
so on. The term "Tier1" usually refers to the tournament metagame,
where you are unlikely to meet a lot of bad players.

Ector
